Name: query_form_retrieval_invariance
Title: Same Fact, Different Doors: Measuring and Repairing Query-Form-Dependent Retrieval in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: The same stored fact is retrieved through partially different internal circuits depending on the surface form of the query (declarative cloze vs. interrogative vs. indirect/paraphrased vs. multiple-choice). We hypothesize that retrieval failures are often not about whether the fact is stored but about whether a given query form successfully 'addresses' the stored location, and that a small set of query-form-specific attention heads act as routers whose failure predicts and causes recall failure across forms.
Related Work: Geva et al. (2023) and Fierro et al. (2024) dissect factual recall as MLP-enrichment plus attention-extraction but use a single declarative form. Hochman et al. (2026) show factual retrieval is distributed/redundant. Elbadry et al. (2026, 'Geometry of Forgetting') show temporal drift is an orthogonal representational axis but do not study query-form dependence. Uncertainty/RAG work (QuCo-RAG 2025, MACR 2026) shows internal confidence is poorly calibrated but operates behaviorally, not mechanistically. Prior paraphrase-robustness studies (e.g., knowledge editing generalization) treat paraphrase variance as an editing nuisance rather than a retrieval-routing phenomenon. Our contribution is the first controlled study that holds the target fact fixed while systematically varying query FORM, quantifies how much the retrieval circuit itself changes across forms, identifies query-form 'router' heads, and tests a form-agnostic intervention that transfers the retrieval pathway from an easy form to a failing form.
Abstract: Language models often answer a fact correctly when it is asked one way and fail when it is asked another—even when the fact is demonstrably stored. We argue this reveals that retrieval in LLMs is query-form-dependent: the same stored association is reached through partially distinct internal pathways depending on whether the query is a declarative cloze, an interrogative question, an indirect paraphrase, or a multiple-choice item. We test this with a matched benchmark where each fact is instantiated in four surface forms with identical target answers, so form varies while content is held fixed. Using logit lens, linear probes, causal activation patching, and attention-knockout, we measure (1) whether the fact is decodable in mid-layers regardless of form (storage invariance) and (2) how much the causal retrieval circuit—the layers/heads that transport the fact to the answer position—differs across forms (retrieval divergence). We identify query-form 'router' heads whose ablation selectively breaks recall for one form but not others, and show their activation predicts per-example success. Finally, we introduce a form-transfer intervention: for a fact the model retrieves correctly in an easy form, we extract the answer-position retrieval direction and inject it while the model processes the failing form, testing whether recall is restored without weight edits and without inducing hallucination on truly-unknown facts. Experiments span Pythia, Qwen2.5, and Llama-3 at multiple scales, measuring storage invariance, retrieval divergence, router-head predictiveness, and repair rate with false-positive controls.
Experiments: 1) BENCHMARK: From CounterFact/T-REx take ~4k facts and instantiate each in 4 matched forms with the SAME single-token (or short) answer: declarative cloze ('The capital of France is __'), interrogative ('What is the capital of France?'), indirect paraphrase ('The city that serves as France's seat of government is __'), and multiple-choice (4 options). Record per-form accuracy; label each fact as STORED using mid-layer probe/logit-lens decodability of the answer at the subject/entity position, independent of output correctness. 2) STORAGE INVARIANCE: Test whether STORED status is form-invariant (probe trained on one form transfers to others; report cross-form probe AUROC). Prediction: high storage invariance, i.e., failures are not storage failures. 3) RETRIEVAL DIVERGENCE: For each form, run causal activation patching (clean vs corrupted entity) to get per-layer/per-head recovery profiles at the answer position; compute pairwise cross-form similarity of these profiles (e.g., cosine of head-contribution vectors). Report a RetrievalDivergence score per fact/model and compare STORED-but-failing vs STORED-and-succeeding items. 4) ROUTER HEADS: Rank attention heads by how selectively their knockout hurts one form vs others (form-selectivity index). Validate that a small set of heads (<10) account for the majority of form-specific breakage; test whether their activation magnitude predicts per-example recall success (AUROC on held-out facts/relations). 5) FORM-TRANSFER INTERVENTION: For facts correct in an easy form but wrong in a hard form, extract the answer-position retrieval direction (difference-of-means of residual at the layer of peak retrieval in the easy form) and add it (scaled by alpha) at the corresponding answer position while processing the hard form. Measure REPAIR RATE (fixed errors), FALSE-POSITIVE rate on genuinely NOT-STORED facts (should not induce confident hallucination), and SIDE EFFECTS on a control set of unrelated queries. Baselines: no intervention, few-shot reformatting, CoT, and generic random-direction injection. 6) GENERALIZATION: Repeat on Pythia (1.4B/6.9B), Qwen2.5 (0.5B/7B), Llama-3 (8B); report whether router heads and divergence patterns are stable across scale/family and whether the transfer direction generalizes across relations. METRICS: per-form accuracy, cross-form storage-probe AUROC, RetrievalDivergence, router-head form-selectivity and predictive AUROC, repair rate, false-positive rate, control accuracy delta.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Probe decodability may overstate 'storage'; we require causal patching corroboration and treat mid-layer decodability as necessary-not-sufficient evidence, cross-validated across forms. 2) Multiple-choice and indirect forms differ in token length/position, confounding patching alignment; we align on the answer/decision position and include token-length-matched paraphrases. 3) Router heads may be polysemantic; we report aggregate selectivity distributions rather than claiming clean one-head-per-form mappings. 4) The transfer intervention may boost hallucination on unknown facts—explicitly measured, with low false-positive rate as a success criterion. 5) Effects may be model/architecture specific (GQA vs MHA); we characterize across families rather than assume universality. 6) Some cross-form failures may reflect genuine reasoning gaps (esp. indirect paraphrases); we restrict causal claims to items with confirmed constituent-fact storage.
